summary: Defines U-NAPTR, a Dynamic Delegation Discovery Service application that maps a domain name to a URI for a particular application service or protocol. It extends the earlier straightforward NAPTR (S-NAPTR) approach, so clients can use DNS to find where a service for a domain actually lives. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: If you know a company's name but not where its chat office is, you can look in a special phone book. This lets computers look up the full address of a service just from the company's name.

questions: how to map a domain to a uri using dns
what is the u flag in naptr
subtitle: A small extension to S-NAPTR that lets DNS records point straight at a URI for a domain's service.

tldr.problem: S-NAPTR finds services for a domain without regular expressions, but that rules out returning a URI. Several applications found this too limiting.
tldr.mechanism: U-NAPTR adds a "U" flag and a tightly limited regular expression of the form !.*!URI! so a NAPTR record can hand back a constant URI.
tldr.outcome: Clients can map a domain to a URI for an application service without implementing full regular expressions.

today: RFC 4848 is a Proposed Standard from April 2007. Its metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why U-NAPTR Exists
sections.content:
RFC 4848 defines a new Dynamic Delegation Discovery Service (DDDS) application called U-NAPTR that maps domain names to URIs for particular application services and protocols. It follows the same principles as S-NAPTR (RFC 3958) and is not an update of it.

S-NAPTR is called straightforward partly because it rules out regular expressions in NAPTR records. That also rules out a URI as the result, which several applications found too limiting. U-NAPTR is a modest extension that allows URIs without allowing the full range of regular expressions.
sections.plainLanguage: The old phone book could only point to another office. This version can also give you a full web-style address, but with a very simple rule for how it is written.

sections.title: The U Flag and Limited Regular Expression
sections.content:
U-NAPTR permits the same flags as S-NAPTR (S, A or empty) plus the new U flag. When U is present, the REGEXP field must be filled in and the REPLACEMENT field is empty.

The regular expression has to be of one form, a complete replacement of the matched string with a constant URI: u-naptr-regexp = "!.*!"<URI>"!", where the URI is as defined in STD 66. The RFC calls this a dodge around the fact that REPLACEMENT can only hold a fully qualified domain name. Applications therefore do not need to implement full regular expression parsers.

The flags are terminal. S means the result is a name that has SRV records, A means look up address records for the name, and U means the result is a URI to resolve. If the flag string is empty, the next lookup is for another NAPTR record. A client that sees any other flag ignores that record and moves on to the next one.
sections.plainLanguage: Each phone book entry has a note saying what kind of answer it holds. The new note, U, says the answer is a ready-made address written in one fixed pattern.

sections.title: Sample Records
sections.content:
The RFC gives sample NAPTR records for example.com, using imagined service tags. WP stands for white pages and EM for an imagined Extensible Messaging service.

  • Order 100, preference 10: service WP:whois++ with an empty flag and a replacement of bunyip.example.com.
  • Order 100, preference 20: service WP:ldap with the s flag and replacement _ldap._tcp.myldap.example.com.
  • Order 200, preference 10: service EM:protA with the u flag and the regexp !.*!prota://someisp.example.com!
  • Order 200, preference 30: service EM:protB with the a flag and replacement myprotB.example.com.
sections.plainLanguage: Here are four sample phone book lines. Each one says what service it is and how to find it, and only one of them gives a full address directly.

sections.title: The Formal DDDS Application Definition
sections.content:
Section 4 fills in the parts a DDDS application must define. The Application Unique String is a fully qualified domain name for which an authoritative server for a service is sought. The First Well Known Rule is identity, so its output is that same name. The expected output is what is needed to connect to the authoritative servers (host, port, protocol or URI).

Service parameters follow an ABNF of an optional app-service followed by any number of app-protocol parts separated by :. Tags are limited to 32 characters, must start with a letter, and are case-insensitive. Names starting with x- are experimental. The separator is a colon because +, the separator in the URI DDDS application, is a valid character in URI scheme names.

The only database specified is the NAPTR DNS record from RFC 3403, keyed by domain names. DNS servers MAY add matching NAPTR, SRV or A records to the Additional Information section, and clients are encouraged but not required to check for them.
sections.plainLanguage: This part is the rulebook: what you look up, what the labels may look like, and where the phone book lives, which is DNS.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The document places no requirements on IANA itself. It reuses the existing registries for application service tags and application protocol tags defined in RFC 3958. Tags starting with x- are experimental, with no protection against duplicate use. Other tags are registered under the specification required policy, where the specification must be an RFC of any category.

The defining RFC must describe the tag, its intended usage, interoperability considerations, security considerations and related publications. It may also add restrictions, such as limits on the kinds of URIs returned.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone can invent a tag that starts with x- for testing. Official tags need a written RFC first so there are no mix-ups.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: U-NAPTR has the same security considerations as S-NAPTR (Section 8 of RFC 3958), plus one more: resolving the returned URI has its own implications, covered in the URI specification. With DNSSEC, client software can be confident that the URI is the one the domain's administrator specified. Whether the service reached by that URI is trustworthy is a matter of URI resolution security practices.
sections.plainLanguage: Locked phone book pages prove the address really came from the company. They do not prove the place at that address is safe.
